glossary.Transaminases: Liver enzymes ALT and AST, released into the blood when liver cells are damaged.
glossary.Encephalopathy: Brain dysfunction, here caused by toxins the failing liver cannot clear.
glossary.Jaundice: Yellowing of the skin and eyes from raised bilirubin in the blood.
glossary.Hepatic flap: Another name for asterixis: a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands.
glossary.Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: Infection of ascitic fluid without an obvious abdominal source, a complication of cirrhosis.
glossary.Neutrophilia: Raised neutrophil count in the blood, often from infection or inflammation.
glossary.Hepatic vein: Veins that drain blood out of the liver into the inferior vena cava.
glossary.Thrombosis: Formation of a blood clot inside a vessel.
glossary.Hereditary haemochromatosis: Inherited iron overload that deposits iron in the liver, heart and pancreas.
glossary.Albumin: Main blood protein made by the liver; low levels suggest poor synthetic function.
glossary.Synthetic function: The liver's ability to make proteins such as albumin and clotting factors.
glossary.U&Es: Urea and electrolytes: blood tests of kidney function and sodium and potassium.
glossary.Clotting profile: Blood tests of clotting, including PT, INR and APTT.
glossary.Viral serology: Blood tests for antibodies or antigens to identify viral infection.
glossary.Paracetamol level: Blood concentration of paracetamol, used to judge overdose risk and need for NAC.
glossary.Prophylaxis: Treatment given to prevent a problem from happening or recurring.
glossary.Cefotaxime: IV third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic, an option for SBP.
glossary.Ciprofloxacin: Fluoroquinolone antibiotic, an alternative option for SBP.
glossary.Arterial pH: Acidity of arterial blood measured on a blood gas; below 7.35 is acidosis.
glossary.Creatinine: Waste product cleared by the kidneys; a high level means poor kidney function.
glossary.Refractory ascites: Ascites that does not respond to, or recurs despite, diuretics.
glossary.Variceal haemorrhage: Bleeding from dilated veins (varices) in the oesophagus or stomach caused by portal hypertension.
glossary.Secondary prophylaxis: Treatment to prevent a problem coming back after it has already happened once.
glossary.Diuretics: Drugs that increase urine output to remove excess fluid.
glossary.Electrolytes: Blood salts such as sodium, potassium and magnesium.
glossary.Supportive care: Treatment that keeps the patient stable while the organ recovers or a cure is arranged.
glossary.Metabolic: Relating to the chemical processes of the body, such as handling glucose.
glossary.Detoxification: Removing or neutralising toxins, such as ammonia and drugs.
glossary.Glucose homeostasis: Keeping blood glucose stable; the failing liver cannot, so hypoglycaemia occurs.
glossary.Bilirubin conjugation: The liver attaching glucuronic acid to bilirubin so it can be excreted in bile.
glossary.Blood-brain barrier: Tightly joined vessel walls that control what passes from blood into the brain.
glossary.Neurotransmission: Signalling between nerve cells using chemical messengers.
glossary.Half-life: Time for the level of a substance in the blood to fall by half.
glossary.Necrosis: Death of cells from injury, rather than programmed cell death.
glossary.Sinusoidal congestion: Blood pooling in the liver's sinusoids because it cannot drain out.
glossary.Hypoxia: Too little oxygen reaching the tissues.
glossary.GI bleed: Bleeding anywhere in the gastrointestinal tract.
